fixtures.prompt: Tell me about a time when you experienced a technical disagreement with teammates on architecture or tool selection. How did you resolve it?
fixtures.context: Collaborative hackathon engineering under high time pressure.

ground_truth_answer.situation: During the Hacklanta '26 hackathon at Georgia State University, our 4-person team built Vantrell, an AI investing platform for BTC/ETH paper trading. As repo owner, I faced a major architectural dispute: half the team wanted an all-Python monolithic service for rapid prototyping, while the other half advocated for a pure Rust system for performance.
ground_truth_answer.task: My responsibility was to resolve the dispute swiftly, prevent team friction, and establish an architecture that balanced rapid AI iteration with strict execution safety.
ground_truth_answer.action: I organized a 30-minute structured spike to benchmark both approaches. I demonstrated that while Python was indispensable for rapid LLM agent experimentation, Rust was vastly superior for sub-millisecond execution and risk checks. I proposed a hybrid microservice architecture: Python agents generated trading decisions and communicated via a strict JSON RPC interface to a high-speed Rust layer that handled trade execution, portfolio state, and risk controls.
ground_truth_answer.result: Both factions supported the consensus architecture. We delivered the full working trading platform ahead of the hackathon deadline, completed 100+ simulated paper trades with sub-millisecond risk validation, and earned high marks from judges.

ground_truth_payload.text_response: At the GSU Hacklanta hackathon, I served as repo owner for our 4-person team building Vantrell, an AI crypto trading platform. Our team deadlocked on language selection: two engineers insisted on building everything in Python for development speed, while the other wanted a pure Rust implementation for low-latency safety. I stepped in to de-escalate the debate by reframing the problem around functional requirements rather than personal preference. I conducted a rapid 20-minute benchmark comparing execution speed and development velocity. I then proposed a decoupled boundary: Python agents handle strategy synthesis where rapid prompt engineering and API libraries shine, while a lightweight Rust service enforces risk checks and executes order books. Both team members immediately saw their priorities respected. We implemented the interface via a typed protocol and shipped the project on time, completing over 100 automated paper trades with zero race conditions.
ground_truth_payload.reasoning: Strong behavioral conflict resolution demonstrating technical maturity, objective benchmarking, and consensus building at GSU Hacklanta.

fixtures.prompt: You are the lead automation engineer on a job application assistant pipeline. Two hours before a scheduled executive milestone demo, an automated test reveals an edge-case bug where assessment links from a secondary job portal fail to parse correctly in 5% of cases. The primary core workflow for standard portals works flawlessly. How should you handle this situation? Rank the following actions from Most Effective (1) to Least Effective (4).

options.text: Immediately isolate the bug, add an explicit defensive catch block that flags the secondary portal links as 'Needs Manual Review' rather than crashing, log the exact payload, and proceed with the demo highlighting the primary flow while transparently noting the triage queue.
Quietly disable all automated tests for the secondary portal so the test suite shows 100% green during the executive presentation, planning to fix the bug sometime next week.

Quickly write a targeted regression test for the 5% failure case, implement a surgical regex/URL unwrap fix, run the full test suite to verify no regressions occurred, and communicate the status to stakeholders prior to the demo.
Postpone the entire executive milestone presentation until the edge case can be fully re-architected and stress-tested over the next three business days.

ground_truth_payload.reasoning: C is most proactive (targeted fix with regression test). A is second best (graceful degradation and honest triage). D is disproportionate (canceling demo for a 5% secondary edge case). B is unacceptable (unethical silencing of failing tests).

fixtures.explanation: Action C demonstrates technical excellence, urgency, and test-driven integrity. Action A shows mature risk mitigation and transparency. Action D is an excessive overreaction that damages stakeholder trust. Action B is an egregious breach of engineering ethics and data integrity.

negative_penalties.condition: Ranking option B as first or second
